title: Block close: room for your question
hook: midrash teaches that the text has room for your question too
tomorrow: did the conversation stop when the Talmud was finished?

segments.voice: Yesterday, four children at the seder, each owed a reply that fits, even the one who pushes back. Each child's answer. Today, the last day of reading midrash, and one more child at the table: you.
screen: `EACH CHILD'S ANSWER.` → `ONE MORE AT THE TABLE.`

segments.voice: A secondhand book, and someone else's pencil in the margins: an underline, a question mark, a small "really?" next to a line. Holding a book like that, you're holding a conversation between two strangers and a page. That is what midrash looks like from the inside. So after forty days of it, yesterday's question: is there any room left for yours?
screen: `PENCIL IN THE MARGINS.` → `A CONVERSATION ON A PAGE.` → `ROOM FOR YOURS?`

segments.voice: Look back at this block and every answer started as a question. Why does the wanting double? Why is Rachel heard when Moses isn't? Who stood afar off at the river? What is a Hebrew name doing on Pharaoh's daughter? The text didn't say. Someone asked, and the answer became midrash. In Pirkei Avot, Ben Bag Bag says of the Torah: turn it, and turn it again, for everything is in it. A midrash on Numbers says the Torah has seventy faces. Not one face copied seventy times: seventy ways of looking. And the tradition kept the arguments, not only the winners. That's why you heard Rabbi Meir beside Rabbi Yehuda, and Rabbi Joshua beside Rabban Yochanan. One to tell a friend tonight: the Mishnah explains why it records opinions that lost, so a later court can lean on them someday. So yes, there's room. Midrash doesn't close the text. It shows how to open it: read closely, notice what's odd, ask honestly, stay inside the words. Your question joins everyone who ever leaned over the same page.
screen: `EVERY ANSWER STARTED AS A QUESTION.` · `TURN IT, AND TURN IT AGAIN.` · `SEVENTY FACES.` · `THE LOSING OPINIONS, KEPT.` · then, large: `THERE'S ROOM FOR YOUR QUESTION.`

segments.voice: Pick up a pen and any paper, and choose one line you know, from this block, a psalm, or a prayer. Write it by hand in the middle of the page and leave wide margins. In the margin, write one question you'd ask it, and if one comes, a single line of answer. Feel the pen move; that's a midrash in miniature, and the whole sit is yours for it.
screen: `ONE LINE, IN THE MIDDLE.` · `WIDE MARGINS.` · `YOUR QUESTION, BY HAND.`

segments.voice: Block close: forty days of reading midrash, from the arithmetic of wanting to the four children, and a margin left open for you.
There's room for your question, in the margin, right beside theirs. Forty of forty: the block is done.

screen: `DAY 1607 COUNTS.` → `READING MIDRASH · 40 OF 40.` → `TOMORROW: DID THE CONVERSATION STOP WHEN THE TALMUD WAS FINISHED?`

howItsDone: Jewish study is often done in pairs (chavruta), reading a text aloud and questioning it together; printed pages of the Talmud set the commentaries around the text in the margins.

chat.meaning: Midrash keeps the text open: read closely, notice, ask honestly. There's room for your question, right beside the ones before you.

Ben Bag Bag.meaning: a sage quoted in Pirkei Avot

Pirkei Avot.meaning: Chapters of the Fathers: sayings of the sages

Mishnah.meaning: the early code of Jewish law the Talmud discusses

midrash.meaning: rabbinic stories and readings that fill gaps in the text
